title: Statistical Plots
text:
A statistical plot shows an estimate together with its uncertainty, or checks a model, instead of only the raw data. Each section below answers one question and names what to read in the plot.
library(tidyverse); library(broom); library(patchwork)
ncd <- read_csv("../data/ncd_survey.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(phys_act = factor(phys_act, levels = c("low", "moderate", "high")),
         education = factor(education, levels = c("No schooling", "Primary", "Secondary", "Graduate+")))
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 13))

title: Statistical Plots
text:
Categorical: proportions with confidence intervals

prev <- ncd |> filter(!is.na(education)) |> group_by(education) |>
  summarise(x = sum(htn), n = n()) |>
  mutate(p = x / n,
         lo = map2_dbl(x, n, \(x, n) prop.test(x, n)$conf.int[1]),
         hi = map2_dbl(x, n, \(x, n) prop.test(x, n)$conf.int[2]))
ggplot(prev, aes(x = education, y = p)) +
  geom_pointrange(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), colour = "#2c3e50") +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0("n = ", n)), y = 0.05, size = 3.5, colour = "grey40") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 0.6)) +
  labs(x = "Education", y = "Adults with hypertension (95% CI)", title = "A proportion is an estimate: show its CI")








prop.test() gives a confidence interval for each proportion. The smallest group (no schooling) has the widest interval: read the interval, not only the point.

title: Statistical Plots
section: Continuous: density with quantile shading, histogram with a fitted curve
text:
Continuous: density with quantile shading, histogram with a fitted curve

q <- quantile(ncd$sbp, c(0.25, 0.75))
d <- density(ncd$sbp); dd <- tibble(x = d$x, y = d$y)
p1 <- ggplot(dd, aes(x, y)) + geom_line() +
  geom_area(data = filter(dd, x >= q[1], x <= q[2]), fill = "#3498db", alpha = 0.4) +
  labs(x = "Systolic BP (mmHg)", y = "Density", title = "Middle 50% shaded")
p2 <- ggplot(ncd, aes(sbp)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)), binwidth = 5, fill = "grey80", colour = "white") +
  stat_function(fun = dnorm, args = list(mean = mean(ncd$sbp), sd = sd(ncd$sbp)), colour = "#e74c3c", linewidth = 1) +
  labs(x = "Systolic BP (mmHg)", y = NULL, title = "Normal curve (same mean, SD)")
p1 + p2








The shaded band is the interquartile range (120 to 143 mmHg). The red curve is what a normal distribution with the same mean and SD would look like: here the data follow it closely, with a slightly longer right tail.

title: Statistical Plots
text:
Category vs category: chi-square residuals

tab <- table(ncd$phys_act, ncd$tobacco)
ct <- chisq.test(tab)
as.data.frame(ct$stdres) |> setNames(c("phys_act", "tobacco", "residual")) |>
  ggplot(aes(tobacco, phys_act, fill = residual)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white") +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.1f", residual))) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#3498db", high = "#e74c3c", limits = c(-3, 3)) +
  labs(x = "Tobacco use", y = "Physical activity", fill = "Std. residual",
       title = sprintf("Chi-square p = %.2f: which cells drive it?", ct$p.value))








A standardised residual compares each cell with what independence predicts: beyond about ±2 the cell contributes noticeably. Here no cell comes close, matching the large p-value.

title: Statistical Plots
section: Continuous vs continuous: regression line, correlation matrix, residuals
text:
Continuous vs continuous: regression line, correlation matrix, residuals

m <- lm(sbp ~ bmi, data = ncd)
ggplot(ncd, aes(bmi, sbp)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", colour = "#e74c3c") +
  annotate("text", x = 16, y = 185, hjust = 0, size = 4,
           label = sprintf("SBP = %.0f + %.2f × BMI\nr = %.2f", coef(m)[1], coef(m)[2], cor(ncd$bmi, ncd$sbp, use = "complete.obs"))) +
  labs(x = "BMI (kg/m²)", y = "Systolic BP (mmHg)", title = "The band is the CI of the mean, not of individuals")









library(ggcorrplot)
r <- cor(select(ncd, age, bmi, waist, salt_g, sbp, dbp), use = "pairwise.complete.obs")
ggcorrplot(r, type = "lower", lab = TRUE, lab_size = 3.5, colors = c("#3498db", "white", "#e74c3c"),
           title = "Pairwise correlations")








BMI and waist are almost the same measurement (r close to 1): putting both in one model causes collinearity.

a <- augment(m)
p1 <- ggplot(a, aes(.fitted, .resid)) + geom_point(alpha = 0.3) + geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = 2) +
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE, colour = "#e74c3c") + labs(x = "Fitted SBP", y = "Residual", title = "Residuals vs fitted")
p2 <- ggplot(a, aes(sample = .resid)) + stat_qq(alpha = 0.3) + stat_qq_line(colour = "#e74c3c") +
  labs(x = "Theoretical quantile", y = "Residual quantile", title = "Normal Q-Q")
p1 + p2








A flat smooth around zero (no curve, no funnel) and points near the Q-Q line support a straight-line model with roughly normal residuals.

title: Statistical Plots
section: Visualising model output: a coefficient plot
text:
Visualising model output: a coefficient plot

m2 <- lm(sbp ~ age + sex + bmi + salt_g + tobacco + phys_act, data = ncd)
tidy(m2, conf.int = TRUE) |> filter(term != "(Intercept)") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = estimate, y = fct_reorder(term, estimate))) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = 2) +
  geom_pointrange(aes(xmin = conf.low, xmax = conf.high), colour = "#2c3e50") +
  labs(x = "Difference in systolic BP (mmHg), 95% CI", y = NULL, title = "Adjusted coefficients")








Each row is one coefficient with its 95% CI; intervals crossing the dashed line at 0 are compatible with no difference. Note that coefficients for different units (per year, per kg/m², per category) are not comparable in size.

title: Statistical Plots
section: Category vs continuous: notched box and violin with median and IQR
text:
Category vs continuous: notched box and violin with median and IQR

tt <- t.test(sbp ~ sex, data = ncd)
p1 <- ggplot(ncd, aes(sex, sbp)) + geom_boxplot(notch = TRUE, fill = "grey85") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Systolic BP (mmHg)", title = sprintf("Welch t-test p = %.3f", tt$p.value))
p2 <- ggplot(ncd, aes(phys_act, sbp)) + geom_violin(fill = "grey90") +
  stat_summary(fun = median, fun.min = \(x) quantile(x, 0.25), fun.max = \(x) quantile(x, 0.75), colour = "#e74c3c") +
  labs(x = "Physical activity", y = NULL, title = "Median and IQR")
p1 + p2








The notch is a rough 95% interval for the median; notches that do not overlap suggest the medians differ. Print the actual test (here in the title) rather than stars.

title: Statistical Plots
Statistical Plots
section: Map: a choropleth with statistical class breaks
text:
Map: a choropleth with statistical class breaks

library(sf)
blocks <- st_read("../data/gis/district_blocks.geojson", quiet = TRUE)
br <- quantile(blocks$dengue_per_100k, probs = seq(0, 1, 0.2))
blocks$class <- cut(blocks$dengue_per_100k, breaks = br, include.lowest = TRUE, dig.lab = 3)
ggplot(blocks) + geom_sf(aes(fill = class), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.2) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "OrRd", name = "Per 100,000\n(quintiles)") +
  labs(title = "Five classes with the same number of blocks") + theme_void()








Quintile breaks put the same number of areas in each colour; equal-interval breaks would leave most blocks in one class. State the method in the caption: the choice of breaks changes the story a map tells.

title: Statistical Plots
text:
Checklist








Show
With
Read




A proportion or mean
point + 95% CI
the interval, with the n


A distribution
density/histogram + quantiles or a fitted curve
shape, tails, the middle 50%


A table of counts
standardised residuals
cells beyond ±2


A relationship
scatter + regression line + CI
slope, r, the band is for the mean


A model
residual plots, coefficient plot
patterns in residuals; CIs crossing 0


Groups
notched box, violin + median/IQR
overlap; the test, not stars


Seasonal counts
decomposition
trend vs season vs remainder


Areas
choropleth with stated breaks
the break method

title: Interactive Plots
text:
A static figure is right for a paper. An interactive one helps when readers explore: hover for the exact value of one point, zoom into a busy period, switch groups on and off, or click a district on a map. Interactive figures work in HTML output (a Quarto web page, a dashboard, a Shiny app); in PDF or Word they are not available, so keep a static version for the paper.
This page uses three packages, each an htmlwidget that Quarto embeds in the page: plotly (charts), DT (tables) and leaflet (maps), plus crosstalk to link them. Data: the NCD survey (data/ncd_survey.csv) and the district blocks of the GIS track.
library(tidyverse)
library(plotly)
ncd <- read_csv(c("../data/ncd_survey.csv", "data/ncd_survey.csv")[file.exists(c("../data/ncd_survey.csv", "data/ncd_survey.csv"))][1],
                show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(phys_act = factor(phys_act, levels = c("low", "moderate", "high")))

title: Interactive Plots
text:
1. Any ggplot, made interactive: ggplotly()
Build the plot as usual, then pass it to ggplotly(). The text aesthetic sets what the tooltip shows.

p <- ggplot(ncd, aes(age, sbp, colour = sex,
                     text = paste0("id ", id, "<br>age ", age, "<br>SBP ", sbp, " mmHg<br>BMI ", bmi))) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  labs(x = "Age (years)", y = "Systolic BP (mmHg)", colour = NULL)
ggplotly(p, tooltip = "text")






Hover a point to read its values; drag to zoom; double-click to reset.
Click a legend entry to hide that group, double-click to show it alone.
tooltip = "text" limits the tooltip to the text you wrote; the default lists every aesthetic.

title: Interactive Plots
section: 2. Categories: bars and boxes with hover labels
text:
2. Categories: bars and boxes with hover labels

by_act <- ncd |> group_by(phys_act) |>
  summarise(n = n(), pct = round(100 * mean(htn), 1))
p <- ggplot(by_act, aes(phys_act, pct, text = paste0(pct, "% of ", n, " people"))) +
  geom_col(fill = "#2C5F8D") +
  labs(x = "Physical activity", y = "Hypertension (%)")
ggplotly(p, tooltip = "text")






ggplotly(ggplot(ncd, aes(phys_act, sbp)) + geom_boxplot(fill = "grey85") +
           labs(x = "Physical activity", y = "Systolic BP (mmHg)"))





The box tooltip gives the median, quartiles and fences of each group: useful in a meeting, where nobody can read values off a static axis.

title: Interactive Plots
section: 3. Native plotly: a histogram with a group switch
text:
3. Native plotly: a histogram with a group switch
plot_ly() builds charts directly. Here two overlaid histograms; click a legend entry to compare one sex at a time.

plot_ly(ncd, x = ~bmi, color = ~sex, type = "histogram", alpha = 0.6, nbinsx = 30) |>
  layout(barmode = "overlay", xaxis = list(title = "BMI (kg/m²)"), yaxis = list(title = "People"))

title: Interactive Plots
section: 4. Time: a line with a range slider
text:
4. Time: a line with a range slider

dengue <- read_csv(c("../data/dengue_wards.csv", "data/dengue_wards.csv")[file.exists(c("../data/dengue_wards.csv", "data/dengue_wards.csv"))][1],
                   show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  group_by(date) |> summarise(cases = sum(cases), rain_mm = mean(rain_mm))
plot_ly(dengue, x = ~date, y = ~cases, type = "scatter", mode = "lines", name = "Dengue cases") |>
  layout(xaxis = list(title = NULL, rangeslider = list(visible = TRUE)), yaxis = list(title = "Cases per month"))





Drag the ends of the slider to zoom into one season; the y-axis keeps its scale, so seasons stay comparable.

title: Interactive Plots
text:
5. A searchable table: DT

library(DT)
ncd |> select(id, village, age, sex, bmi, sbp, dbp, htn) |>
  datatable(rownames = FALSE, filter = "top", options = list(pageLength = 5))






filter = "top" adds a filter box above each column; sort by clicking a header.
Use it for lists readers look things up in (facilities, villages); not as a substitute for a summary table.

title: Interactive Plots
text:
6. Linked views: crosstalk
crosstalk::SharedData lets two widgets use the same rows: select points in the scatter plot and the table shows only those people.

library(crosstalk)
shared <- SharedData$new(ncd |> select(id, age, sex, sbp, dbp, bmi))
bscols(widths = c(6, 6),
       plot_ly(shared, x = ~dbp, y = ~sbp, type = "scatter", mode = "markers", alpha = 0.5) |>
         layout(xaxis = list(title = "Diastolic BP"), yaxis = list(title = "Systolic BP")) |>
         highlight(on = "plotly_selected", off = "plotly_deselect"),
       datatable(shared, rownames = FALSE, options = list(pageLength = 6, dom = "tp")))















Choose the box select tool (top right of the plot), drag over the points with high systolic BP, and the table lists who they are. This works in a static HTML page: no server is needed.

title: Interactive Plots
text:
7. Maps: leaflet

library(leaflet); library(sf)
blocks <- st_read(c("../data/gis/district_blocks.geojson", "data/gis/district_blocks.geojson")[file.exists(c("../data/gis/district_blocks.geojson", "data/gis/district_blocks.geojson"))][1],
                  quiet = TRUE)
pal <- colorNumeric("YlOrRd", blocks$dengue_per_100k)
leaflet(blocks) |>
  addProviderTiles(providers$CartoDB.Positron) |>
  addPolygons(fillColor = ~pal(dengue_per_100k), fillOpacity = 0.8, color = "white", weight = 1,
              label = ~block_name,
              popup = ~paste0("<b>", block_name, "</b><br>Population: ", format(population, big.mark = ","),
                              "<br>Dengue: ", dengue_per_100k, " per 100,000")) |>
  addLegend(pal = pal, values = ~dengue_per_100k, title = "Dengue per 100k")






Hover a block for its name; click it for the popup.
The base map tiles load from the internet; the shaded blocks do not need a connection.
Mapping rules (class breaks, rates rather than counts) are in the GIS track.

title: Interactive Plots
text:
When to use interactivity







Use it when
Avoid it when




Readers explore many points or groups
The figure has one message: a static plot says it faster


Exact values matter on hover
The output is PDF, Word or print


Dashboards, teaching, data checking
Hiding information behind a hover that every reader needs









TipChecklist




Keep a static version for the paper; the interactive one goes in the supplement or a web appendix.
Write the tooltip yourself: units, rounding, the n.
Large data (more than about 50,000 points) makes the page slow: summarise first, or use toWebGL().
Save a widget as its own file with htmlwidgets::saveWidget(widget, "fig.html").
Other packages: ggiraph (interactive ggplot2 layers), highcharter, echarts4r; Shiny when a reader should change the analysis, not just the view.

title: Practical Application
text:
Publication Figure - Code


Code
library(readxl); library(ggplot2); library(ggeffects)
health_data <- read_excel("../data/PublicHealth_BP_Dataset.xlsx")    # 200 simulated patients
model <- lm(SysBP_6m ~ TreatmentGroup + Age + BMI + SysBP_0m, data = health_data)
effects <- ggpredict(model, terms = "TreatmentGroup")

p <- plot(effects, colors = "bw") +
  labs(title = "Treatment effect on systolic blood pressure",
       subtitle = "Adjusted for age, BMI and baseline BP",
       x = "Treatment group", y = "Predicted systolic BP at 6 months (mmHg)",
       caption = "Error bars: 95% confidence intervals. n = 100 per group.") +
  theme_bw(base_size = 12) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", hjust = 0), panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
p



Code
# Save for the journal (in a project: "output/figures/figure1.tiff")
ggsave(file.path(tempdir(), "figure1.tiff"), p, width = 7, height = 5, dpi = 300, compression = "lzw")

title: Relational/Flow - INTERMEDIATE
text:
What We’ll Learn - Intermediate


Visualizing Relationships:

Network diagrams (nodes & edges)
Sankey diagrams (flow)
Chord diagrams (circular relationships)
Alluvial plots (categorical flows)
Correlation networks


Analytical Goals:

🔴 Flow - Movement between states
⚫ Correlation - Strength of relationships
🟢 Ranking - Most connected nodes
🟡 Distribution - Network properties

title: Relational/Flow - INTERMEDIATE
text:
Setup Code


Code
# Load required packages
library(readxl)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(tidyr)
library(igraph)      # For network analysis
library(ggraph)      # For network visualization
library(networkD3)   # For Sankey diagrams
library(circlize)    # For chord diagrams

# Load datasets
health_data <- read_excel("../../data/PublicHealth_BP_Dataset.xlsx")
network_data <- read_excel("../../data/Healthcare_Network_Dataset.xlsx", sheet = 2)

# Create custom theme
theme_custom <- function() {
  theme_void() +  # Clean background for networks
  theme(
    text = element_text(family = "serif", size = 12),
    plot.title = element_text(size = 16, face = "bold", hjust = 0.5),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 11, hjust = 0.5),
    legend.position = "right"
  )
}

Network Diagram Basics - Code

Purpose: Show relationships between entities (nodes)

Code
# Prepare network data (patient referrals between providers)
edges <- network_data %>%
  select(from = FromProvider, to = ToProvider, 
           weight = NumReferrals) %>%
  filter(!is.na(from), !is.na(to), weight > 0)

# Create network graph object
network_graph <- graph_from_data_frame(edges, directed = TRUE)

# Calculate node importance (degree centrality)
V(network_graph)$degree <- degree(network_graph)
V(network_graph)$betweenness <- betweenness(network_graph)

# Plot network
ggraph(network_graph, layout = "fr") +  # Fruchterman-Reingold layout
  geom_edge_link(aes(width = weight, alpha = weight),
                arrow = arrow(length = unit(3, "mm")),
                end_cap = circle(3, "mm"),
                color = "gray60") +
  geom_node_point(aes(size = degree, color = degree)) +
  geom_node_text(aes(label = name), repel = TRUE, size = 3) +
  scale_edge_width(range = c(0.5, 3)) +
  scale_edge_alpha(range = c(0.3, 0.8)) +
  scale_size(range = c(3, 10)) +
  scale_color_viridis_c(option = "plasma") +
  labs(title = "Healthcare Provider Referral Network",
       subtitle = "Node size = number of connections | Arrow width = referral volume",
       size = "Connections",
       color = "Connections") +
  theme_custom()

text:
Sankey Diagram - Code

Purpose: Show flow quantities between stages
Goal: 🔴 Flow + 🔴 Part of Whole


Code
# Prepare flow data: Patient journey through treatment
# Stage 1: Initial Assessment → Stage 2: Treatment Selection → Stage 3: Outcome

# Create flow data
flow_data <- health_data %>%
  filter(!is.na(TreatmentGroup), !is.na(Adherence_Status)) %>%
  count(TreatmentGroup, Adherence_Status, name = "count") %>%
  # Rename for Sankey format
  rename(source = TreatmentGroup, target = Adherence_Status, value = count)

# Prepare nodes and links for networkD3
nodes <- data.frame(
  name = unique(c(as.character(flow_data$source), 
                 as.character(flow_data$target)))
)

# Create links with node indices
flow_data$IDsource <- match(flow_data$source, nodes$name) - 1  # 0-indexed
flow_data$IDtarget <- match(flow_data$target, nodes$name) - 1

# Create Sankey diagram
sankeyNetwork(
  Links = flow_data,
  Nodes = nodes,
  Source = "IDsource",
  Target = "IDtarget",
  Value = "value",
  NodeID = "name",
  units = "patients",
  fontSize = 14,
  nodeWidth = 30,
  sinksRight = FALSE,  # Align target nodes to left
  colourScale = JS('d3.scaleOrdinal().domain(["Treatment A", "Treatment B", "Control", "High", "Low"]).range(["#E41A1C", "#377EB8", "#4DAF4A", "#FF7F00", "#984EA3"])')
)


Note: This creates an interactive HTML widget

# Prepare chord data: Comorbidity co-occurrence

  filter(!is.na(PatientRegion), !is.na(TreatmentAssigned)) %>%

  grid.col = c("North" = "#E41A1C", "South" = "#377EB8",

text:
Correlation Network - Code

Purpose: Visualize correlation patterns as network
Goal: ⚫ Correlation + clustering


Code
# Calculate correlations among numeric health metrics
cor_data <- health_data %>%
  select(Age, BMI_0m, SysBP_0m, DiaBP_0m, 
         Cholesterol_0m, BloodSugar_0m) %>%
  cor(use = "complete.obs")

# Convert to network (only strong correlations)
cor_network <- cor_data %>%
  as.data.frame() %>%
  mutate(from = rownames(.)) %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = -from, names_to = "to", values_to = "correlation") %>%
  filter(from != to, abs(correlation) > 0.3) %>%  # Threshold
  mutate(abs_cor = abs(correlation))

# Create graph
cor_graph <- graph_from_data_frame(cor_network, directed = FALSE)
E(cor_graph)$weight <- cor_network$abs_cor
E(cor_graph)$cor_sign <- ifelse(cor_network$correlation > 0, "Positive", "Negative")

# Plot
ggraph(cor_graph, layout = "fr") +
  geom_edge_link(aes(width = abs_cor, color = cor_sign), alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_node_point(size = 10, color = "#4DBBD5") +
  geom_node_text(aes(label = name), size = 3.5, color = "white", fontface = "bold") +
  scale_edge_width(range = c(1, 4)) +
  scale_edge_color_manual(values = c("Positive" = "#00A087", "Negative" = "#DC0000")) +
  labs(title = "Health Metrics Correlation Network",
       subtitle = "Edge width = correlation strength | Color = positive/negative",
       edge_color = "Correlation",
       edge_width = "Strength") +
  theme_custom()

text:
Common Mistakes


Too many nodes/edges

Solution: Filter to top connections, increase threshold

Poor layout choice

Solution: Try different layouts (fr, kk, circle, tree)

Unreadable labels

Solution: Use repel = TRUE, adjust size, or interactive plots

Ignoring direction in networks

Solution: Use arrows for directed graphs

Color overload in complex diagrams

Solution: Limit to 2-3 colors, use grayscale for edges

Not showing flow magnitude clearly

Solution: Vary width, transparency, or both

# Calculate summary statistics
summary_data <- health_data %>%
  filter(!is.na(Gender), !is.na(ExerciseFreq), !is.na(BMI)) %>%
  group_by(Gender, ExerciseFreq) %>%
  summarise(
    mean_bmi = mean(BMI, na.rm = TRUE),
    se_bmi = sd(BMI, na.rm = TRUE) / sqrt(n()),
    n = n(),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  mutate(ExerciseFreq = factor(ExerciseFreq,
                              levels = c("Never", "1-2 days/week",
                                       "3-4 days/week", "5-7 days/week")))

# Create grouped bar chart with error bars and sample sizes

  geom_col(position = position_dodge(0.9), alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = mean_bmi - se_bmi, ymax = mean_bmi + se_bmi),
                position = position_dodge(0.9), width = 0.25) +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0("n=", n)), 
            position = position_dodge(0.9), vjust = -1.5, size = 3) +
  labs(title = "Mean BMI by Exercise Frequency and Gender",
       subtitle = "Error bars show ± 1 SE | Numbers show sample size",

When to use facets: When you have 3+ categorical variables to compare

Common Mistakes to Avoid


Too many groups in one plot

Solution: Use facets or filter to top groups

Ignoring sample size differences

Solution: Show n on plot or use error bars

Comparing distributions without uncertainty

Solution: Add confidence intervals or error bars

Bee swarms with too many points

Solution: Use violin or density if n > 500

Not ordering categories logically

Solution: Order by median, mean, or natural order

Forgetting about color-blind audiences

Solution: Use color-blind safe palettes (viridis, ColorBrewer)

text:
Missing Data Handling

Always check for missing data:


Code
# Check missing data by group
health_data %>%
  group_by(Gender, ExerciseFreq) %>%
  summarise(
    total = n(),
    missing_bmi = sum(is.na(BMI)),
    pct_missing = round(100 * missing_bmi / total, 1)
  )


Options for handling:

Filter complete cases - filter(!is.na(variable))
Show as separate category - useful if missing is informative
Note in subtitle - “Excludes N missing observations”
Investigate patterns - Is missingness related to outcome?

Lollipop Chart - Code
🟢 Goal: Ranking (cleaner alternative to bars)


Code
# Calculate counts and prepare for ordered lollipop
region_counts <- data_clean %>%
  count(Region) %>%
  arrange(n)  # Sort for proper ordering

# Create lollipop chart
ggplot(region_counts, aes(x = n, y = fct_reorder(Region, n))) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = 0, xend = n, y = Region, yend = Region),
               color = "gray70", size = 1.5) +  # Draw lollipop sticks
  geom_point(size = 5, color = "#2C5F8D") +  # Draw lollipop heads

       x = "Number of Patients", y = "Region") +
  theme_minimal(base_family = "serif") +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, size = 16, face = "bold"),
        axis.title = element_text(size = 12),
        panel.grid.major.y = element_blank())  # Remove horizontal grid

title: Categorical Plots - INTERMEDIATE
text:
Reading Lollipop and Dot Plots
Using the previous plot:

OBSERVATION: - North region: widest column (33% of patients); East narrowest (20%) - Treatment share differs by region: Intervention 68% in East, 47% in North, 38% in South, 51% in West - The horizontal edges do not line up across columns - Chi-square test of Region × Treatment: p ≈ 0.05 (borderline)
INTERPRETATION: - Width of columns: regional sample sizes (North > South ≈ West > East) - Height within columns: treatment allocation within each region - Misaligned edges: allocation was not the same in every region - If this were a trial, region would need to be checked as a possible imbalance
IMPLICATIONS: - Report allocation by region, not only overall - Consider adjusting for region in the analysis - A mosaic shows this at a glance; a single overall percentage would hide it
Reading Mosaic Tips: - Misaligned tiles = association exists - Aligned tiles = independence (no association) - Area, not just height, represents proportion - Compare conditional distributions (within columns)

title: Categorical Plots - INTERMEDIATE
text:
Complex Mosaic - Code
🔴 Goal: Multi-way categorical analysis


Code
# Three-way mosaic drawn as rectangles (a mosaic is just rectangles):
# width = patients in each Gender : Treatment column, height = smoking shares
tiles <- data_clean %>%
  filter(Gender %in% c("Male", "Female")) %>%
  count(Gender, TreatmentGroup, SmokingStatus) %>%
  mutate(column = paste(Gender, TreatmentGroup, sep = " : ")) %>%
  group_by(column) %>%
  mutate(ymax = cumsum(n) / sum(n), ymin = ymax - n / sum(n)) %>%
  ungroup()
cols <- tiles %>% count(column, wt = n, name = "col_n") %>%
  mutate(xmax = cumsum(col_n), xmin = xmax - col_n)
tiles <- left_join(tiles, cols, by = "column")

ggplot(tiles) +
  geom_rect(aes(xmin = xmin, xmax = xmax, ymin = ymin, ymax = ymax,
                fill = SmokingStatus), colour = "white", linewidth = 1) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = (cols$xmin + cols$xmax) / 2, labels = cols$column) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Current smoker" = "#E74C3C",
                                "Former smoker" = "#F39C12",
                                "Non-smoker" = "#27AE60"),
                    name = "Smoking Status") +
  labs(title = "Smoking Status by Gender and Treatment Group",
       x = "Gender : Treatment Group (width = number of patients)", y = "Proportion") +
  theme_minimal(base_family = "serif") +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, size = 15, face = "bold"))

  mutate(ExerciseFreq = fct_reorder(ExerciseFreq, n))

# Create radial bar chart
ggplot(exercise_counts, aes(x = ExerciseFreq, y = n, fill = ExerciseFreq)) +
  geom_col(alpha = 0.8, color = "white", size = 1) +  # Create bars
  coord_polar(theta = "y") +  # Transform to circular coordinates
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2", name = "Exercise Frequency") +
  geom_text(aes(label = n), position = position_stack(vjust = 0.5),
            family = "serif", size = 5, fontface = "bold") +  # Add labels
  labs(title = "Exercise Frequency Distribution (Radial)",
       x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_family = "serif") +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, size = 16, face = "bold"),
        axis.text = element_blank(),

title: Categorical Plots - INTERMEDIATE
text:
Key Takeaways

When to use each: - Lollipop > Bar: When you have many categories or want cleaner look - Cleveland Dot: Perfect for before/after or male/female comparisons
- Mosaic: Test if two categorical variables are independent - Radial: Use sparingly (harder to read), good for presentations
Pro Tips: - fct_reorder() from forcats package is essential for proper ordering - Mosaic aligned tiles = independent, misaligned = associated - Remove gridlines for cleaner lollipop charts - Always label mosaic plot axes clearly (area = proportion!)
Common Mistakes: - Using radial charts for data without circular nature - Too many categories in mosaic plots (>12 becomes unreadable) - Not ordering lollipop charts by value - Misinterpreting mosaic plots (height alone doesn’t show proportion)

title: Time Series - BASIC
text:
What is Time Series Data?


Definition:
Data points indexed by time or ordered sequence

Observations at regular intervals
Temporal ordering matters
Shows change over time
Can reveal trends and patterns


Examples in Our Dataset:

Blood Pressure at 0, 3, 6 months
Patient measurements over time
Baseline dates
Treatment progression
Longitudinal health outcomes

title: Time Series - BASIC
text:
Analytical Goals for Time Series

What questions can we answer?

🔵 Evolution - How does it change over time?
🟡 Distribution - What’s the pattern across time periods?
🟢 Ranking - Which time period is highest/lowest?

Charts we’ll learn:

Simple Line Chart
Multiple Line Chart (comparing groups)
Line Chart with Points

title: Time Series - BASIC
text:
Setup: Load and Prepare Data


Code
# Load required libraries
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)      # For data reshaping

# Load the dataset
data <- readxl::read_excel("../../data/PublicHealth_BP_Dataset.xlsx")

# Reshape data from wide to long format for time series plotting
# Convert columns SysBP_0m, SysBP_3m, SysBP_6m to rows
bp_long <- data %>%
  select(PatientID, TreatmentGroup, SysBP_0m, SysBP_3m, SysBP_6m) %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = starts_with("SysBP"),
               names_to = "TimePoint",
               values_to = "SysBP") %>%  # Convert to long format
  mutate(Month = case_when(TimePoint == "SysBP_0m" ~ 0,
                           TimePoint == "SysBP_3m" ~ 3,
                           TimePoint == "SysBP_6m" ~ 6))  # Extract month number

# Preview the transformed data
head(bp_long)

Simple Line Chart - Code
🔵 Goal: Show evolution over time (aggregate)


Code
# Calculate mean systolic BP at each time point
mean_bp <- bp_long %>%
  group_by(Month) %>%
  summarise(Mean_SysBP = mean(SysBP, na.rm = TRUE))  # Average across all patients

# Create line chart showing trend over time
ggplot(mean_bp, aes(x = Month, y = Mean_SysBP)) +
  geom_line(color = "steelblue", size = 1.5) +  # Draw line
  geom_point(color = "steelblue", size = 4) +  # Add points at each time point
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, 3, 6)) +  # Show all time points on x-axis
  labs(title = "Mean Systolic Blood Pressure Over 6 Months",
       x = "Month", 
       y = "Mean Systolic BP (mmHg)") +
  theme_minimal(base_family = "serif") +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, size = 16, face = "bold"),
        axis.title = element_text(size = 12),
        axis.text = element_text(size = 10))

text: Simple Line Chart - Plot

title: Time Series - BASIC
text:
How to Read Line Charts
Using the previous plot:

OBSERVATION: - Baseline (Month 0): mean systolic BP 135.1 mmHg - Month 3: 132.2 mmHg (2.9 mmHg lower) - Month 6: 130.4 mmHg (another 1.8 mmHg lower) - Steady downward trend, no rebound
INTERPRETATION: - Mean blood pressure fell by about 5 mmHg over six months - This line mixes both groups: it cannot say whether the intervention caused the fall
IMPLICATIONS: - Plot the groups separately (next slide): the Control mean stays at about 136 mmHg, the Intervention mean falls from 134 to 125 mmHg - An overall mean can hide that only one group changed - A change over time is not a treatment effect without a comparison group
ACTIONS: - Always show a line per group in a trial - Add error bars or confidence intervals before drawing conclusions

title: Time Series - BASIC
text:
Multiple Line Chart - Code
🔵 Goal: Compare evolution across groups


Code
# Calculate mean BP by treatment group and time
mean_bp_group <- bp_long %>%
  group_by(Month, TreatmentGroup) %>%
  summarise(Mean_SysBP = mean(SysBP, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

# Create line chart with separate lines for each group
ggplot(mean_bp_group, aes(x = Month, y = Mean_SysBP, 
                          color = TreatmentGroup, group = TreatmentGroup)) +
  geom_line(size = 1.5) +  # Draw lines
  geom_point(size = 4) +  # Add points
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Control" = "#E74C3C", 
                                 "Intervention" = "#3498DB"),
                     name = "Treatment Group") +  # Custom colors
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, 3, 6)) +
  labs(title = "Systolic BP by Treatment Group Over Time",
       x = "Month", y = "Mean Systolic BP (mmHg)") +
  theme_minimal(base_family = "serif") +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, size = 16, face = "bold"),
        axis.title = element_text(size = 12),
        legend.position = "right")

title: Time Series - BASIC
section: Line Chart with Error Bars - Code
text:
Line Chart with Error Bars - Code
🔵 Goal: Show trend with uncertainty


Code
# Calculate mean and standard error by group
bp_summary <- bp_long %>%
  group_by(Month, TreatmentGroup) %>%
  summarise(Mean_SysBP = mean(SysBP, na.rm = TRUE),
            SE = sd(SysBP, na.rm = TRUE) / sqrt(n()),  # Standard error
            .groups = "drop")

# Create line chart with error ribbons
ggplot(bp_summary, aes(x = Month, y = Mean_SysBP, 
                       color = TreatmentGroup, fill = TreatmentGroup)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = Mean_SysBP - SE, ymax = Mean_SysBP + SE),
              alpha = 0.2, color = NA) +  # Add confidence bands
  geom_line(size = 1.5) +  # Draw lines on top
  geom_point(size = 4) +  # Add points
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Control" = "#E74C3C", 
                                 "Intervention" = "#3498DB")) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Control" = "#E74C3C", 
                                "Intervention" = "#3498DB")) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, 3, 6)) +
  labs(title = "Systolic BP Over Time with Standard Error",
       x = "Month", y = "Mean Systolic BP (mmHg)") +
  theme_minimal(base_family = "serif") +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, size = 16, face = "bold"),
        legend.position = "right")

Goal
When to Use

title: Time Series - BASIC
text:
Key Time Series Concepts


Trend: - Overall direction (up, down, flat) - Long-term pattern - Calculate: moving average, regression
Seasonality: - Regular periodic fluctuations - Daily, weekly, monthly patterns - Example: Higher BP in winter
Volatility: - Amount of variation - High = unstable, Low = stable - Measure: standard deviation

Data Preparation: - Wide format: One column per time point - Long format: One row per observation - Use pivot_longer() to convert
Best Practices: - Always show all time points - Use consistent time intervals - Label axes clearly with units - Consider adding reference lines - Show confidence intervals when relevant

title: Time Series - BASIC
text:
Key Takeaways

Remember:

Connect the dots - use geom_line() to show continuity
Add points - helps identify exact time points
Multiple lines need legends - make groups clear
Show uncertainty - confidence intervals add credibility
Wide to long format - essential for time series plotting

Common Mistakes:

Not connecting points (scatter instead of line)
Too many lines (>5 becomes cluttered)
Inconsistent time intervals without noting
Missing baseline comparisons
Not handling missing time points

Histogram - Code
🟡 Goal: Distribution (show frequency across bins)


Code
# Create histogram showing age distribution
ggplot(data_clean, aes(x = Age)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "steelblue", color = "white", alpha = 0.8) +  # 30 bins
  labs(title = "Distribution of Patient Ages",

  theme_minimal(base_family = "serif") +  # Serif font for professional look

title: Continuous Plots - BASIC
text: Histogram - Plot

title: Continuous Plots - BASIC
text:
How to Read Histograms
Using the previous plot:

OBSERVATION: - Ages range from 18 to 79 years (median 50) - Patients are spread over the whole range, with somewhat more between 45 and 55 - No single sharp peak and no long tail - No gaps and no impossible values
INTERPRETATION: - The study covers the whole adult age range - No age group dominates the sample - Age is not normally distributed, but that does not matter for using it as a predictor
IMPLICATIONS: - Results can be described across adult ages - Age can be used as a continuous variable; groups (e.g. 18–39, 40–59, 60+) are only for description - Every age band has enough patients for a description
ACTIONS: - Consider age as a covariate in treatment analyses - Change bins and check the picture does not depend on it

title: Continuous Plots - BASIC
text:
Histogram with Mean/Median Lines - Code
🟡 Goal: Distribution with central tendency markers


Code
# Calculate summary statistics
age_mean <- mean(data_clean$Age, na.rm = TRUE)  # Calculate mean
age_median <- median(data_clean$Age, na.rm = TRUE)  # Calculate median

# Create histogram with reference lines
ggplot(data_clean, aes(x = Age)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "steelblue", color = "white", alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = age_mean), color = "red", 
             linetype = "dashed", size = 1) +  # Add mean line
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = age_median), color = "darkgreen", 
             linetype = "solid", size = 1) +  # Add median line
  annotate("text", x = age_mean + 5, y = 15, 
           label = paste("Mean =", round(age_mean, 1)), 
           color = "red", family = "serif", size = 4) +  # Label mean
  annotate("text", x = age_median - 5, y = 15, 
           label = paste("Median =", round(age_median, 1)), 
           color = "darkgreen", family = "serif", size = 4) +  # Label median
  labs(title = "Age Distribution with Mean and Median",
       x = "Age (years)", y = "Frequency") +
  theme_minimal(base_family = "serif") +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, size = 16, face = "bold"))

text:
Scatter Plot - Code
⚫ Goal: Correlation between two continuous variables


Code
# Create scatter plot showing BMI vs. Cholesterol relationship
ggplot(data_clean, aes(x = BMI, y = Cholesterol)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6, color = "darkblue", size = 3) +  # Add semi-transparent points
  labs(title = "Relationship between BMI and Cholesterol",
       x = "Body Mass Index (BMI)", y = "Cholesterol (mg/dL)") +
  theme_minimal(base_family = "serif") +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, size = 16, face = "bold"),
        axis.title = element_text(size = 12))




alpha = 0.6 makes points semi-transparent to show overlapping
Look for patterns: positive correlation, negative, or no relationship

title: Continuous Plots - BASIC
text: Scatter Plot - Plot

title: Continuous Plots - BASIC
text:
How to Read Scatter Plots
Using the previous plot:

OBSERVATION: - Points are scattered over the whole plot - No linear pattern (correlation r = 0.00, p = 0.97) - BMI ranges from 11.4 to 37.3; cholesterol from 151 to 299 mg/dL - A few BMI values below 15 sit far to the left
INTERPRETATION: - No association between BMI and cholesterol in this sample - BMI values below 15 are implausible for adults: check them before any analysis
IMPLICATIONS: - BMI alone does not predict cholesterol here - Other factors (diet, genetics, medication) are likely to matter - A scatter plot is the first data-quality check, not only a picture of association

title: Continuous Plots - BASIC
text:
Scatter Plot with Categories - Code
⚫ Goal: Correlation + Compare groups


Code
# Scatter plot colored by Treatment Group
ggplot(data_clean, aes(x = Age, y = SysBP_0m, color = TreatmentGroup)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7, size = 3) +  # Color points by group
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Control" = "#E74C3C", 
                                 "Intervention" = "#3498DB"),
                     name = "Treatment Group") +  # Custom colors
  labs(title = "Baseline Systolic BP by Age and Treatment Group",
       x = "Age (years)", 
       y = "Systolic Blood Pressure (mmHg)") +
  theme_minimal(base_family = "serif") +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, size = 16, face = "bold"),
        axis.title = element_text(size = 12),
        legend.position = "right")

title: Continuous Plots - BASIC
text:
Common Distribution Shapes


Normal (Bell Curve) - Symmetric around mean - Mean ≈ Median - Example: Heights
Right Skewed - Long tail to the right - Mean > Median
- Example: Income
Left Skewed - Long tail to the left - Mean < Median - Example: Age at retirement

Bimodal - Two peaks - Two distinct groups - Example: Customer segments
Uniform - Flat distribution - All values equally likely - Example: Random numbers
Outliers - Extreme values - Check for data errors - May need special handling

title: Continuous Plots - BASIC
text:
Key Takeaways

Remember:

Choose bins wisely - test different values for histograms
Density vs. Histogram - density better for comparing groups
Scatter plots reveal relationships - but don’t assume causation
Alpha transparency - helps see overlapping points
Always handle missing data - document your approach

Common Mistakes:

Too many/few histogram bins
Not handling outliers
Assuming correlation = causation
Ignoring data transformations when needed
Poor color choices for scatter plot groups

title: Dashboards - ADVANCED

Dashboard Layout Principles


F-Pattern Layout:

Top row: Key metrics (KPIs)
Left column: Filters/controls
Center: Main visualizations
Right: Secondary insights

Golden Rules:

Most important info top-left
Limit to 5-7 visualizations
Consistent color scheme
Clear hierarchy


Example Structure:
┌─────────────────────────────┐
│ KPI 1  │ KPI 2  │ KPI 3     │
├────────┼────────┼───────────┤
│ Filter │ Main Chart         │
│ Panel  │                    │
│        ├────────────────────┤

└────────┴────────────────────┘

title: Network - ADVANCED
text:
Topics Covered

Community detection algorithms
Centrality measures visualization
Network statistics
Dynamic networks
Bipartite networks

Goal: Advanced network insights

title: Network - ADVANCED
text:
Setup
Data: 20 providers and 74 referral links between them, January to June (data/Healthcare_Network_Dataset.xlsx, simulated).


Code
library(readxl); library(tidyverse); library(igraph); library(ggraph)
providers <- read_excel("../../data/Healthcare_Network_Dataset.xlsx", sheet = "Providers")
referrals <- read_excel("../../data/Healthcare_Network_Dataset.xlsx", sheet = "Referrals")

edges <- referrals |> transmute(from = FromProvider, to = ToProvider, weight = NumReferrals, Month, ReferralType)
nodes <- providers |> transmute(name = ProviderID, label = sprintf("P%02d", ProviderID), Specialty, Region)
net <- graph_from_data_frame(edges, directed = TRUE, vertices = nodes)

title: Network - ADVANCED
text:
Community Detection


Code
set.seed(42)
communities <- cluster_louvain(as_undirected(net, edge.attr.comb = list(weight = "sum", "ignore")))
V(net)$community <- factor(membership(communities))
ggraph(net, layout = "fr") +
  geom_edge_link(aes(width = weight), alpha = 0.25, colour = "grey40") +
  geom_node_point(aes(colour = community), size = 5) +
  geom_node_text(aes(label = label), repel = TRUE, size = 3) +
  scale_edge_width(range = c(0.3, 2), guide = "none") +
  scale_colour_brewer(palette = "Dark2", name = "Community") +
  labs(title = "Provider communities (Louvain)") +
  theme_void()



Louvain groups providers who refer more to each other than to the rest; the groups can change with the random seed, so treat them as a hypothesis, not a fact.

title: Network - ADVANCED
text:
Centrality Measures


Code
V(net)$degree <- degree(net, mode = "all")
V(net)$betweenness <- betweenness(net, normalized = TRUE, weights = NA)   # weights would be read as distances
ggraph(net, layout = "kk") +
  geom_edge_link(alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_node_point(aes(size = betweenness, colour = degree)) +
  geom_node_text(aes(label = label), repel = TRUE, size = 3) +
  scale_colour_viridis_c() +
  labs(title = "Provider centrality", subtitle = "Size = betweenness | Colour = degree") +
  theme_void()



Degree = how many links; betweenness = how often a provider sits on the shortest path between two others (a broker: if they are absent, referrals take longer routes).

title: Network - ADVANCED
text:
Network Statistics Table


Code
stats <- tibble(
  Metric = c("Providers (nodes)", "Referral links (edges)", "Density", "Mean path length",
             "Clustering coefficient", "Modularity of the communities"),
  Value = c(vcount(net), ecount(net), round(edge_density(net), 3), round(mean_distance(net, weights = NA), 2),
            round(transitivity(net), 3), round(modularity(communities), 3)))
knitr::kable(stats)





Metric
Value




Providers (nodes)
20.000


Referral links (edges)
74.000


Density
0.195


Mean path length
2.310


Clustering coefficient
0.355


Modularity of the communities
0.289





Density = links present / links possible. A modularity near 0 means the communities are weak.

title: Network - ADVANCED
text:
Bipartite Network


Code
bip <- referrals |> group_by(from = sprintf("P%02d", FromProvider), to = ReferralType) |>
  summarise(weight = sum(NumReferrals), .groups = "drop")
bp_net <- graph_from_data_frame(bip, directed = FALSE)
V(bp_net)$type <- V(bp_net)$name %in% bip$to                 # TRUE = referral type
ggraph(bp_net, layout = "bipartite") +
  geom_edge_link(aes(width = weight), alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_node_point(aes(colour = type), size = 4) +
  geom_node_text(aes(label = name), size = 2.5, vjust = -1.2) +
  scale_edge_width(range = c(0.2, 2), guide = "none") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = "#2C5F8D", `TRUE` = "#E67E22"),
                      labels = c("Provider", "Referral type"), name = NULL) +
  labs(title = "Who sends which kind of referral") +
  theme_void()



Two kinds of node, and links only between kinds: providers and the referral types they send.

title: Network - ADVANCED
text:
Dynamic Network (Time-based)


Code
library(patchwork)
set.seed(1)
coords <- create_layout(net, layout = "fr")[, c("x", "y")]        # same positions in both panels
half <- function(months, title) {
  sub <- subgraph_from_edges(net, E(net)[Month %in% months], delete.vertices = FALSE)
  ggraph(sub, layout = "manual", x = coords$x, y = coords$y) +
    geom_edge_link(alpha = 0.4) + geom_node_point(colour = "#2C5F8D", size = 2.5) +
    labs(title = title) + theme_void()
}
half(c("Jan", "Feb", "Mar"), "January–March") + half(c("Apr", "May", "Jun"), "April–June")



Fixing the node positions makes the two periods comparable: only the links change.

title: Category vs Continuous - ADVANCED
text:
Topics Covered

Effect plots (model-based)
Interaction plots
Marginal effects
Bayesian credible intervals
Mixed effects visualization

Goal: Show complex statistical relationships

title: Category vs Continuous - ADVANCED
text:
Setup
Data: 200 simulated patients of a blood-pressure trial (data/PublicHealth_BP_Dataset.xlsx, see data/README.md).


Code
library(readxl); library(dplyr); library(ggplot2)
library(ggeffects); library(interactions); library(broom)
health_data <- read_excel("../../data/PublicHealth_BP_Dataset.xlsx")
model <- lm(SysBP_6m ~ TreatmentGroup * Gender + Age + BMI + SysBP_0m, data = health_data)


The model adjusts the 6-month SBP for baseline SBP, age and BMI, and lets the treatment effect differ by gender.

title: Category vs Continuous - ADVANCED
text:
Interaction Plot


Code
cat_plot(model, pred = TreatmentGroup, modx = Gender, interval = TRUE, int.width = 0.95,
         geom = "point") +
  labs(title = "Treatment effect by gender", y = "Predicted systolic BP at 6 months") +
  theme_minimal()



The intervention lowers SBP by about 9 mmHg in every gender group; the interaction test agrees (anova(model), row TreatmentGroup:Gender: p = 0.67). Test an interaction, do not judge it by eye.

title: Category vs Continuous - ADVANCED
text:
Marginal Effects Plot


Code
effects <- ggpredict(model, terms = c("Age [all]", "TreatmentGroup"))
plot(effects) +
  labs(title = "Age and predicted SBP at 6 months, by treatment group",
       x = "Age (years)", y = "Predicted SBP (mmHg)") +
  theme_minimal()



Model-based predictions with confidence bands, other variables held at their mean or reference level.

title: Category vs Continuous - ADVANCED
text:
Forest Plot (Effect Sizes)


Code
coef_data <- tidy(model, conf.int = TRUE) |> filter(term != "(Intercept)")
ggplot(coef_data, aes(x = estimate, y = reorder(term, estimate))) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_errorbar(aes(xmin = conf.low, xmax = conf.high), width = 0.2, orientation = "y") +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  labs(title = "Regression coefficients with 95% CI", x = "Difference in SBP at 6 months (mmHg)", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()



Standard in medical research. Coefficients on different scales (per year of age vs per group) are not comparable in size.

title: Category vs Continuous - ADVANCED
text:
Raincloud by Multiple Groups


Code
library(ggdist)
health_data |>
  filter(!is.na(TreatmentGroup), !is.na(Gender)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = Gender, y = SysBP_6m, fill = Gender)) +
  stat_halfeye(adjust = 0.6, width = 0.5, justification = -0.25, .width = 0, point_colour = NA) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.12, outlier.shape = NA) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.05, alpha = 0.3, size = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~ TreatmentGroup) +
  labs(y = "Systolic BP at 6 months (mmHg)", x = NULL) +
  theme_minimal() + theme(legend.position = "none")



Distribution, summary and raw data at once, for nested groups.

title: Category vs Continuous - ADVANCED
text:
Bayesian Credible Intervals


Code
library(rstanarm)
bayes_model <- stan_glm(SysBP_6m ~ TreatmentGroup + Age + SysBP_0m, data = health_data,
                        chains = 2, iter = 1000, seed = 2026, refresh = 0)
plot(bayes_model, pars = c("TreatmentGroupIntervention", "Age", "SysBP_0m"), prob = 0.5, prob_outer = 0.95) +
  labs(title = "Posterior estimates (50% and 95% credible intervals)")



A 95% credible interval holds the coefficient with 95% probability, given the model and its (weak, default) priors.

title: Categorical - ADVANCED
text:
Setup Code


Code
# Load required packages
library(readxl)
library(tidyverse)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(treemapify)  # For treemaps
library(sunburstR)   # For sunburst charts

# Load dataset
health_data <- read_excel("../../data/PublicHealth_BP_Dataset.xlsx")

# Create hierarchical data
hierarchical_data <- health_data %>%
  filter(!is.na(Region), !is.na(Gender), !is.na(SmokingStatus)) %>%
  count(Region, Gender, SmokingStatus, name = "count")

# Create theme
theme_custom <- function() {
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    text = element_text(family = "serif", size = 12),
    plot.title = element_text(size = 16, face = "bold", hjust = 0.5),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 11, hjust = 0.5),
    legend.position = "bottom"
  )
}

title: Categorical - ADVANCED
text:
Treemap - Code

Purpose: Show hierarchical part-to-whole relationships
Goal: 🔴 Part of Whole + 🟢 Ranking


Code
# Prepare data for treemap
treemap_data <- health_data %>%
  filter(!is.na(Region), !is.na(TreatmentGroup)) %>%
  count(Region, TreatmentGroup, name = "count") %>%
  mutate(label = paste0(TreatmentGroup, "\n(n=", count, ")"))

# Create treemap
ggplot(treemap_data, aes(area = count, fill = Region, 
                         label = label, subgroup = Region)) +
  geom_treemap() +
  geom_treemap_subgroup_border(color = "white", size = 3) +
  geom_treemap_subgroup_text(
    place = "center",
    grow = TRUE,
    alpha = 0.5,
    color = "black",
    fontface = "bold",
    size = 18
  ) +
  geom_treemap_text(
    color = "white",
    place = "center",
    size = 10,
    grow = FALSE
  ) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2") +
  labs(title = "Patient Distribution by Region and Treatment",
       subtitle = "Rectangle size proportional to patient count",
       fill = "Region") +
  theme_custom() +
  theme(legend.position = "right")

title: Categorical - ADVANCED
text: Treemap - Output

title: Categorical - ADVANCED
text:
Interpreting Treemaps


Key Features:

Size = Quantity - Larger rectangles = more patients
Color = Category - Each region has its own color
Hierarchy - Region (outer) → Treatment (inner)
Space-efficient - Uses all available area

Best Practices:

Limit to 2-3 hierarchy levels
Use clear labels
Consistent color scheme
Consider interactivity for complex trees


Our Treemap Shows:

East region largest overall

Most patients

Within each region treatment distribution visible

Relative sizes easy to compare

Quick identification of smallest/largest segments
Hierarchical structure immediately clear

Region → Treatment breakdown


Advantage: Efficient use of space compared to nested pie charts

title: Categorical - ADVANCED
text:
Sunburst Chart - Code

Purpose: Radial hierarchical visualization
Goal: 🔴 Part of Whole (circular)


Code
# Prepare data in required format for sunburst
# Format: path-count pairs
sunburst_data <- health_data %>%
  filter(!is.na(Region), !is.na(Gender), !is.na(SmokingStatus)) %>%
  count(Region, Gender, SmokingStatus) %>%
  mutate(path = paste(Region, Gender, SmokingStatus, sep = "-")) %>%
  select(path, n)

# Create sunburst chart
sunburst(
  data = sunburst_data,
  count = TRUE,
  legend = list(w = 150, h = 25, s = 5, t = 25),
  breadcrumb = list(w = 0, h = 25, s = 5, t = 10),
  colors = list(
    range = c("#E41A1C", "#377EB8", "#4DAF4A", "#984EA3",
             "#FF7F00", "#FFFF33", "#A65628", "#F781BF")
  ),
  withD3 = TRUE,
  width = "100%",
  height = 500
)


Note: Sunburst creates interactive HTML widget. For static, use ggplot2 alternative.
Static Alternative (next slide):

title: Categorical - ADVANCED
text:
Sunburst Alternative: Radial Bar - Code



Code
# Create radial bar plot (sunburst alternative)
radial_data <- health_data %>%
  filter(!is.na(Region), !is.na(SmokingStatus)) %>%
  count(Region, SmokingStatus) %>%
  group_by(Region) %>%
  mutate(
    percentage = n / sum(n) * 100,
    id = paste(Region, SmokingStatus, sep = "-")
  )

ggplot(radial_data, aes(x = Region, y = n, fill = SmokingStatus)) +
  geom_col(width = 1, color = "white", size = 0.5) +
  coord_polar() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Never" = "#00A087", 
                              "Former" = "#3C5488",
                              "Current" = "#DC0000")) +
  labs(title = "Smoking Status Distribution by Region (Radial)",
       subtitle = "Each segment shows proportion within region",
       fill = "Smoking Status") +
  theme_custom() +
  theme(
    axis.text.y = element_blank(),
    axis.title = element_blank(),
    panel.grid = element_blank()
  )

text: Radial Bar - Output

title: Categorical - ADVANCED
text:
Marimekko Chart - Code

Purpose: Two-way composition (varying column widths)
Goal: 🔴 Part of Whole (two dimensions)


Code
# Prepare data for Marimekko
marimekko_data <- health_data %>%
  filter(!is.na(Region), !is.na(TreatmentGroup)) %>%
  count(Region, TreatmentGroup) %>%
  group_by(Region) %>%
  mutate(
    region_total = sum(n),
    pct_in_region = n / region_total * 100
  ) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(
    region_pct = region_total / sum(region_total) * 100,
    cumsum_region = cumsum(region_pct) - region_pct / 2
  )

# Create Marimekko chart
ggplot(marimekko_data, aes(x = Region, y = pct_in_region, 
                           fill = TreatmentGroup, width = region_pct)) +
  geom_col(position = "stack", color = "white", size = 0.5) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set1") +
  labs(title = "Treatment Distribution by Region (Marimekko)",
       subtitle = "Column width = regional patient share | Height = treatment proportion",
       x = "Region",
       y = "Percentage within Region",
       fill = "Treatment") +
  theme_custom() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 0))

Interpreting Marimekko Charts

Unique Features:

Two dimensions of composition

Width would represent one variable’s total
Height shows breakdown within that category

Space = Area

Total area of each segment = actual count contribution

Compare both dimensions simultaneously

More information dense than standard stacked bars

title: Categorical - ADVANCED
text:
Waffle Chart - Code

Purpose: Unit-based visualization (each square = fixed count)
Goal: 🔴 Part of Whole (intuitive units)


Code
# Prepare data (each unit = 10 patients)
waffle_data <- health_data %>%
  filter(!is.na(TreatmentGroup)) %>%
  count(TreatmentGroup) %>%
  mutate(squares = round(n / 10))  # 1 square = 10 patients

# Create waffle chart
waffle_expanded <- waffle_data %>%
  rowwise() %>%
  mutate(id = list(1:squares)) %>%
  unnest(id) %>%
  mutate(square_id = row_number(),
         x = (square_id - 1) %% 10,   # 10 rows
         y = (square_id - 1) %/% 10)

# Plot with ggplot2
ggplot(waffle_expanded, aes(x = x, y = y, fill = TreatmentGroup)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white", size = 0.5) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Treatment A" = "#E41A1C",
                               "Treatment B" = "#377EB8",
                               "Control"     = "#4DAF4A")) +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(title = "Patient Distribution by Treatment Group",
       x = "1 square = 10 patients",
       y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    axis.text.y = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks = element_blank(),
    text = element_text(family = "serif", size = 12),
    plot.title = element_text(size = 16, face = "bold", hjust = 0.5)
  )

Why Waffle Charts Work:

Intuitive unit representation

Each square = fixed count (e.g., 10 patients)
Easy to count and compare

Avoid pie chart problems

No angles to judge
Better for exact comparisons

Visual impact

Engaging and memorable
Good for presentations and infographics

title: Categorical - ADVANCED
text:
Dendrogram - Code

Purpose: Show hierarchical clustering of categories
Goal: ⚫ Correlation + hierarchical structure


Code
# Calculate dissimilarity matrix for regions based on health metrics
region_profiles <- health_data %>%
  filter(!is.na(Region)) %>%
  group_by(Region) %>%
  summarise(
    mean_bp = mean(SysBP_0m, na.rm = TRUE),
    mean_chol = mean(Cholesterol_0m, na.rm = TRUE),
    mean_bmi = mean(BMI_0m, na.rm = TRUE),
    pct_smokers = mean(SmokingStatus == "Current", na.rm = TRUE) * 100
  ) %>%
  column_to_rownames("Region")

# Scale variables
region_scaled <- scale(region_profiles)

# Hierarchical clustering
hc <- hclust(dist(region_scaled), method = "ward.D2")

# Plot dendrogram
library(ggdendro)
ggdendrogram(hc, rotate = FALSE, theme_dendro = FALSE) +
  labs(title = "Hierarchical Clustering of Regions by Health Profiles",
       subtitle = "Based on BP, cholesterol, BMI, and smoking rates",
       x = "Region",
       y = "Distance (Ward's method)") +
  theme_custom() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 0))

Interpreting Dendrograms


Reading Dendrograms:

Height = Dissimilarity
Branches joining lower = more similar
Clusters formed by cutting at height
Leaf = Individual category

Method Matters:

Ward’s - Minimizes within-cluster variance
Complete - Maximum distance
Average - Mean distance between clusters


Our Dendrogram:

East and North most similar

Join at lowest height
Similar health profiles

South different from North/East

Joins at higher level

West most distinct

Joins last, highest dissimilarity


Use Case: Identifying similar market segments, patient groups

title: Plotting Tools
text:
This chapter introduces various tools and libraries available in R for creating visualizations. It covers base R plotting functions, as well as popular packages like ggplot2 and lattice, which offer advanced capabilities for creating complex and customizable plots.


R’s built-in plotting functions provide a solid foundation for data visualization:


# Scatter plot
plot(x = mtcars$wt, y = mtcars$mpg,
     xlab = "Weight", ylab = "Miles per Gallon",
     main = "Scatter Plot Example")

# Line plot
plot(x = 1:10, y = (1:10)^2, type = "l",
     xlab = "X", ylab = "Y^2")

# Bar plot
barplot(height = c(10, 15, 8, 12),
        names.arg = c("A", "B", "C", "D"))

# Histogram
hist(mtcars$mpg, breaks = 10,
     xlab = "Miles per Gallon",
     main = "Histogram of MPG")



# Multiple plots in one window
par(mfrow = c(2, 2))  # 2x2 grid

plot(mtcars$wt, mtcars$mpg)
hist(mtcars$mpg)
boxplot(mtcars$mpg ~ mtcars$cyl)
plot(density(mtcars$mpg))

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))  # Reset to single plot




ggplot2 is the most popular R package for data visualization, based on the Grammar of Graphics:


library(ggplot2)

# Basic scatter plot
ggplot(data = mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) +
  geom_point()

# Adding aesthetics
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg, color = factor(cyl))) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  labs(title = "MPG vs Weight by Cylinders",
       x = "Weight (1000 lbs)",
       y = "Miles per Gallon")



# Points, lines, bars
p <- ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg))

p + geom_point()           # Scatter plot
p + geom_smooth()          # Smooth line
p + geom_line()            # Line plot
p + geom_bar(stat = "identity")  # Bar plot
p + geom_histogram()       # Histogram
p + geom_boxplot()         # Box plot



# Faceting
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) +
  geom_point() +
  facet_wrap(~ cyl) +
  theme_minimal()

# Custom themes
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) +
  geom_point() +
  theme_bw() +
  ggtitle("Custom Theme Example")




Lattice provides trellis graphics for multivariate data:
library(lattice)

# Scatter plot matrix
splom(mtcars[, c("mpg", "wt", "hp")])

# Conditional plots
xyplot(mpg ~ wt | factor(cyl), data = mtcars,
       layout = c(3, 1))

# 3D plots
cloud(mpg ~ wt * hp, data = mtcars)





library(plotly)

# Convert ggplot to interactive
p <- ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) + geom_point()
ggplotly(p)

# Native plotly
plot_ly(mtcars, x = ~wt, y = ~mpg, type = "scatter", mode = "markers")



library(ggvis)

# Interactive ggplot2-like syntax
mtcars %>%
  ggvis(x = ~wt, y = ~mpg) %>%
  layer_points() %>%
  add_tooltip(function(df) paste("Weight:", df$wt, "MPG:", df$mpg))






library(ggstatsplot)

# Statistical plots with tests
ggbetweenstats(data = mtcars, x = cyl, y = mpg)



library(ggplot2)
library(maps)

# Basic map
world <- map_data("world")
ggplot(world, aes(x = long, y = lat, group = group)) +
  geom_polygon(fill = "lightblue", color = "black")



library(igraph)
library(ggraph)

# Create network
g <- make_ring(10)
ggraph(g, layout = "circle") +
  geom_edge_link() +
  geom_node_point(size = 5)





Base R: Quick plots, statistical graphics
ggplot2: Publication-quality static plots, complex customizations
Lattice: Multivariate data, trellis displays
plotly/ggvis: Interactive web-based visualizations
Specialized packages: Domain-specific visualizations (maps, networks, etc.)





Know your data: Choose plot types that best represent your data
Keep it simple: Avoid clutter, focus on the message
Use color effectively: Consider colorblind-friendly palettes
Label clearly: Include informative titles, axis labels, legends
Test different tools: Experiment with different packages for the best result

A plot with two y-axes on one x
Saving one plot into four files

Draws one panel per number of cylinders
Colours the points by number of cylinders

title: Debugging Plots
text:
Debugging plots are essential tools for diagnosing issues in data visualization and analysis. They help identify problems such as incorrect data representation, scaling issues, or unexpected patterns in the data. In this guide, we will explore various techniques and tools for creating effective debugging plots.





Missing or incorrect data types
# Check data types
str(mtcars)

# Check for missing values
sum(is.na(mtcars))

# Visualize missing patterns
library(naniar)
vis_miss(mtcars)
Outliers affecting scales
# Check for outliers
boxplot(mtcars$mpg)

# Use robust statistics
library(robustbase)
summary(mtcars$mpg)





Mapping vs Setting Aesthetics
# Correct: Map color to variable
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg, color = factor(cyl))) +
  geom_point()

# Incorrect: Setting color globally
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) +
  geom_point(color = "red")  # This sets all points to red
Factor Level Issues
# Check factor levels
levels(mtcars$cyl)

# Reorder factors if needed
mtcars$cyl <- factor(mtcars$cyl, levels = c("4", "6", "8"))
Geom Conflicts
# Error: Can't use geom_bar with y aesthetic
# ggplot(data, aes(x = category, y = value)) + geom_bar()

# Correct: Use stat = "identity"
ggplot(data, aes(x = category, y = value)) + 
  geom_bar(stat = "identity")







# Check ggplot object structure
p <- ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) + geom_point()
str(p)

# View plot data
p$data
p$mapping



# Build plot incrementally
p1 <- ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg))
print(p1)  # Should show empty plot

p2 <- p1 + geom_point()
print(p2)  # Check if points appear

p3 <- p2 + theme_minimal()
print(p3)  # Check theme application



# Enable ggplot2 debugging
options(ggplot2.debug = TRUE)

# Check for warnings
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) + geom_point()






# Problem: Length mismatch
# ggplot(data, aes(x = x_var, y = y_var, color = short_vector))

# Solution: Ensure vectors are same length or use single values
ggplot(data, aes(x = x_var, y = y_var, color = factor(category)))



# Problem: Wrong scale type
# ggplot(data, aes(x = factor_var, y = numeric_var)) + scale_x_continuous()

# Solution: Use appropriate scale
ggplot(data, aes(x = factor_var, y = numeric_var)) + scale_x_discrete()



# Problem: Typo in parameter name
# geom_point(size = 3)  # Correct
# geom_point(siz = 3)   # Incorrect

# Solution: Check documentation
?geom_point






# Residual plots for model diagnostics
model <- lm(mpg ~ wt, data = mtcars)
plot(model)

# QQ plots for normality
qqnorm(mtcars$mpg)
qqline(mtcars$mpg)



# Correlation plots
library(corrplot)
corrplot(cor(mtcars))

# Pairs plots
pairs(mtcars[, c("mpg", "wt", "hp")])



# Plot data distributions
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = mpg)) + 
  geom_histogram() + 
  facet_wrap(~ cyl)

# Check for data issues
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) + 
  geom_point() + 
  geom_text(aes(label = rownames(mtcars)), check_overlap = TRUE)






# When plot fails
tryCatch({
  ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) + geom_point()
}, error = function(e) {
  print(e)
  traceback()
})



library(profvis)

# Profile plotting code
profvis({
  p <- ggplot(large_dataset, aes(x = x, y = y)) + geom_point()
  print(p)
})



# Check memory usage
gc()

# For large datasets, use sampling
sample_data <- mtcars[sample(nrow(mtcars), 1000, replace = TRUE), ]
ggplot(sample_data, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) + geom_point()





Start simple: Build plots incrementally
Check data first: Validate input data before plotting
Use reproducible examples: Create minimal examples that reproduce issues
Read error messages carefully: They often point to the exact problem
Check package versions: Ensure compatible versions of ggplot2 and extensions
Use debugging tools: Leverage R’s debugging functions and ggplot2’s debug options
Document fixes: Keep notes on solutions for future reference

R Graphics Cookbook by Winston Chang
ggplot2 book by Hadley Wickham
Stack Overflow ggplot2 tag
RStudio Community forums

# Check for data issues
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) + 
  geom_point() + 
  geom_text(aes(label = rownames(mtcars)), check_overlap = TRUE)

title: Navigating the Decision Tree
section: Quick Reference - What Each Color Means
text:
Quick Reference - What Each Color Means

● Gold/Yellow = Distribution - Shows data spread, frequency, shape, outliers
● Blue = Correlation - Shows relationships, associations between variables
● Green = Ranking - Shows order, comparison of values, top/bottom
● Red/Salmon = Part of Whole - Shows composition, proportions, percentages
● Light Blue = Evolution - Shows trends, changes over time, trajectories
● Purple = Maps - Shows geographic/spatial distribution, location-based data
● Pink/Tan = Flow - Shows movement, transitions, journeys, hierarchies

Tip: When you see a colored dot next to a chart name, it tells you what analytical goal that chart serves best!

The 6 Data Type Categories








Data Type

Ordered categories
